articles.title: Why Europe doesn’t need another Silicon Valley to succeed | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Since AI became mainstream, comparisons between Europe’s innovation hubs and Silicon Valley have become ever-present.
In 2026, the EU was still debating domestic cloud capacity, Big Tech dependence, and the energy demands of new data centres.
As investors, we keep hearing the same question from European founders: should they build from Europe, move closer to the US market, or try to do both? Europe’s opportunity is selective ambition. It should understand where the AI infrastructure race rewards US scale and focus on the layers where it already has an advantage.
The AI infrastructure reality
Before AI, a talented software team could build a large product with modest infrastructure. AI changed that. Frontier model companies compete for GPUs, data-centre capacity, energy access, research talent, and large pools of capital. Balance sheets, supply chains, and infrastructure partnerships matter as much as product.
European founders have to price this into strategy. Energy costs, slow data-centre permitting and fragmented capital markets may improve, but not at the speed of the current AI infrastructure cycle.
That makes specialisation more important: the strongest AI companies from Europe may sit where domain expertise, customer access, regulation and workflow ownership matter more than compute.
Why many European startups still look west
The attractiveness of the American technology market remains strong. Capital, customers, acquirers, and commercial talent still concentrate there. Seed and Series A capital in Europe is now more achievable than a decade ago, but growth rounds often require a stronger US connection.
Opening a US office is simple compared to the commercial work that follows. Enterprise software companies need people who understand US procurement and know how to create urgency inside large organisations. Europe has no shortage of talented operators.
The constraint is narrower: the region has produced fewer enterprise software companies that repeatedly sold into large US customers at scale, so the pool of executives with that specific go-to-market experience is still limited.
This is where valuation expectations become dangerous. A European company cannot claim US-style multiples because its deck lists American competitors. If revenue is still European, most investors will usually continue to see the company as European. The US valuation story becomes credible when American customers represent a meaningful part of the business.
For instance, we once saw a profitable Eastern European business open a New York office and hire talent from competitors. Yet, the firm still struggled, because the founding team had not spent enough time inside the market.
The first 18 to 24 months in the US are not really expansion yet. They are the time founders need to learn how the market works: how buyers frame the problem, how sales conversations move, how competitors position themselves.
Where Europe genuinely wins
The right strategy depends on what a company is building. Defence and security technology are good examples. Yes, the American market is larger, but when you consider procurement rules, nationality questions, compliance requirements, and cap-table concerns, successfully entering can be much harder than expected.
Sometimes, the barrier sits in procurement and compliance rather than product quality. A startup with investors from politically sensitive geographies may find US government or defence customers difficult to approach until the cap table is cleaned up. For that company, a Europe-first path, or a different international route, can be better than forcing a Silicon Valley narrative.
Industrial software is another area where Europe has an advantage that is difficult to copy. A startup building in this space benefits from proximity to factories, procurement teams, and technical buyers.
Applied AI can follow the same logic. A company building AI for logistics, manufacturing, energy, compliance, healthcare operations, or industrial maintenance may gain more from expert customers than from proximity to the largest venture funds. In those markets, the moat often comes from workflow knowledge, proprietary customer context, and trust.
The signs we look for
When a European founder comes with a US expansion question, the conversation usually starts with three practical checks: who they need to sell to, who can sell it, and whether the company has enough US proof to support its fundraising story.
If the next constraint is product depth, domain knowledge, regulated customer access, manufacturing proximity, or defence procurement, Europe may remain the right centre of gravity.
If it is growth capital, enterprise sales velocity, senior go-to-market hiring, or access to acquirers, the company probably needs a stronger US presence. The signal is practical: European customer concentration points to Europe; US buyers asking for local references or growth investors requiring proof of US demand point to America.
What Europe needs to get right
Europe’s challenge is not international expansion. Great companies go where customers, capital, and talent are. The task is making Europe attractive for companies that have a reason to stay.
That starts by removing barriers that hinder founders from scaling. One example is taxing paper wealth. A founder can raise a round at a high valuation and look wealthy on paper while still holding illiquid shares and putting every available resource back into the company.
If the system treats that mark-up as liquid wealth, a fundraising milestone can become a personal cash problem.
Hiring is another example. We have seen a company find a strong C-level candidate in Spain and decide not to hire him because the employment framework made a high-risk senior hire too hard to unwind if the fit was wrong.
Here, Europe lost more than one role; it lost a chance to turn a local executive into someone inside a global technology company. These are the frictions Europe needs to reduce.
The continent does not need to win every layer of the AI stack. It needs to win the layers where customer intimacy, regulatory understanding, engineering depth, industrial know-how, and trust matter more than raw compute.
There is a large market in that space, and European founders are better positioned to capture it than they are often given credit for.

articles.title: 20+ Hijacked Government Websites Became an Attack Channel
articles.text:
More than 20 Brazilian government websites were hijacked and turned into malware delivery channels in an active PhantomEnigma campaign uncovered by ANY.RUN, a leading provider of interactive malware analysis and threat intelligence solutions.
The investigation revealed previously undocumented backdoor behavior, hidden infrastructure relationships, and multiple attack arms behind a campaign putting banks and public agencies at risk.
By connecting hundreds of seemingly unrelated sandbox sessions, ANY.RUN researchers exposed the operation’s broader scope and showed how trusted .gov.br links and authenticated emails helped the activity remain hidden.
For the complete technical analysis, infrastructure details, indicators, and detection guidance, read the full PhantomEnigma investigation report
Trusted Government Infrastructure Became the Lure
The attack began with fake police-themed documents presented as official “Ofício Polícia Civil” or “Procuração Digital” notices. Some contained QR codes, while others directed recipients to links designed to look like legitimate government resources.
| Fake police-themed document analyzed inside ANY.RUN sandbox for full visibility into PhantomEnigma attack | 
In several cases, the emails were sent through compromised mailboxes and passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks. That gave the messages a stronger appearance of legitimacy than ordinary spoofed phishing emails.
Victims were then redirected through compromised .gov.br hosts or police-themed lookalike domains before reaching the malicious installer. The government systems were used as trusted delivery infrastructure, not necessarily as the final targets of the campaign.
Observed Government Hosts
Among the compromised systems observed during the investigation were timon.ma.gov[.]br, loginam.sesp.es.gov[.]br (state public security), aplicacao.cbm.mt.gov[.]br (fire department), prodoc.ap.gov[.]br, and others.
| TI Lookup query that involves compromised government hosts | 
These legitimate municipal, public-security, and judicial portals were used at different stages of the delivery chain. Several also appeared across more than one PhantomEnigma attack arm, helping researchers connect activity that initially looked unrelated.
PhantomEnigma’s Evolution: Two Paths to Harder Detection
| Timeline of PhantomEnigma’s malisious activity | 
The timeline shows one operation evolving along two main paths:
Delivery: PhantomEnigma moved from banking-focused activity in 2025 to abusing compromised .gov.br websites and email accounts in 2026. This gave the campaign a more trusted route to victims without confirming a new target group.
Arsenal: The malware evolved from a browser-extension banker into a modular Inno/Node.js backdoor capable of executing JavaScript and delivering additional payloads.
For security teams, this combination creates a serious visibility gap. Trusted infrastructure reduces suspicion, modular payloads can change after infection, and rotating C2 domains quickly make static blocklists outdated. Behavioral analysis and continuous threat hunting provide more reliable coverage as the campaign evolves.
From Trusted Email to Full Compromise: The PhantomEnigma Attack Chain
| The analysis process of PhantomEnigma inside interactive sandbox | 
Once a victim engaged with the lure, the campaign moved through a multi-stage infection chain:
- Phishing email: A fake police-themed or official-document lure reaches the victim.
- Trusted infrastructure: The link redirects through a compromised government host or police-themed lookalike domain.
- Malicious installer: An Inno Setup, MSI, or another installer starts the infection.
- Patched Electron application: Legitimate software loads a malicious index.js backdoor.
- Backdoor activation: The malware collects system data, establishes persistence, and connects to rotating C2 infrastructure.
- Second-stage delivery: The backdoor executes JavaScript or delivers stealers, loaders, RMM software, and other malware.
- Business impact: The infection can lead to credential compromise, unauthorized access, fraud, data exposure, and operational disruption.
What Researchers Found Inside PhantomEnigma’s Backdoor
The sandbox sessions exposed more than a simple downloader. Hidden inside a patched Boostnote and other applications was a modular index.js backdoor built to identify infected machines, maintain access, and deliver different payloads on demand.
Once activated, the backdoor could:
- Collect the victim’s computer name, username, and system details
- Create a persistent machine ID and read a campaign tag stored beside the installer
- Establish persistence through login settings
- Check for new commands every 180 seconds
- Execute JavaScript directly through eval()
- Download and launch executable payloads
- Communicate through multiple beacon formats across rotating infrastructure
This modular design allows the operator to change the final payload without rebuilding the entire infection chain. A system initially exposed to the same installer could later receive a stealer, loader, remote management tool, or another executable, making both detection and containment more difficult.
A Warning for Banks and Public Agencies
PhantomEnigma shows how attackers can turn trusted infrastructure into a detection advantage. A legitimate government domain, authenticated email, or clean file verdict may lower suspicion even when the infection chain is already active.
For banks and public-sector organizations, the risk extends beyond one compromised endpoint. Stolen credentials and persistent backdoor access can expose internal systems, sensitive data, and financial operations, while fragmented alerts delay containment.
Security teams should give employees a safe way to report suspicious official-looking messages and investigate them beyond the initial verdict. Catching the trusted lure early can prevent credential theft, additional payload delivery, and a wider operational incident.
Get PhantomEnigma IOCs, infrastructure findings, and detection guidance to strengthen threat hunting and response.

articles.title: Usuários relatam aumento de anúncios no YouTube, até no Premium Lite • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Usuários relatam aumento de anúncios no YouTube, até no Premium Lite
Usuários reclamam de excesso de anúncios no YouTube. Em alguns casos, serviço exibiu três comerciais seguidos no começo do vídeo.
Usuários reclamam de excesso de anúncios no YouTube. Em alguns casos, serviço exibiu três comerciais seguidos no começo do vídeo.
Estaria o YouTube exibindo mais anúncios do que antes ou com intervalos menores entre eles? Até o momento, não há nenhum comunicado oficial sobre isso, mas os relatos sobre esse comportamento têm crescido nos últimos dias.
É o que observa o Android Authority, que encontrou, via Reddit, várias queixas sobre um aparente excesso de anúncios no YouTube. Na maioria dos casos, os usuários reclamam que a plataforma de streaming tem exibido três anúncios seguidos no início de cada vídeo, sendo que a quantidade típica é de até dois anúncios iniciais.
Também há relatos de um aumento na quantidade de anúncios que são exibidos no decorrer do vídeo. Esse comportamento fez o intervalo entre os anúncios diminuir para algo entre três e quatro minutos em alguns casos.
Para piorar a situação, há, entre eles, anúncios que não podem ser pulados. Sobre isso, chama a atenção o relato de um usuário que afirma ter encontrado um anúncio com mais de 9 minutos de duração que era exibido sem o botão de pular anúncio. Nessas circunstâncias, é preciso sair e entrar no vídeo novamente para se desvencilhar do conteúdo “invasor”.
Também chamou a atenção o relato de um usuário que afirma que a quantidade de anúncios exibidos para assinantes do YouTube Premium Lite também aumentou. Outros usuários responderam concordando com a afirmação.
Essa opção de plano remove a maioria das propagandas, mas ainda pode exibi-las em Shorts ou em conteúdos musicais, por exemplo. O contrassenso aqui é que, se o número de anúncios do YouTube Premium Lite aumentar consideravelmente, acaba não havendo sentido em assinar esse plano.
É difícil saber. Talvez o Google esteja apenas testando a tolerância dos usuários a mais anúncios ou, então, esteja preparando a plataforma para, de fato, exibir mais publicidade.
O Android Authority pediu explicações sobre o assunto à companhia, mas não houve retorno até o momento.
Para muitos usuários, a saída tem sido a de recorrer a bloqueadores de anúncios, sejam eles fornecidos por meio de extensões ou por recursos nativos dos navegadores. Nesse sentido, o navegador do DuckDuckGo traz justamente o bloqueio de anúncios do YouTube como a principal novidade de sua versão mais recente.
Assinar o YouTube Premium continua sendo a alternativa oficial para quem deseja escapar das propagandas da plataforma. Além de inibir anúncios, a modalidade oferece recursos como reprodução em segundo plano e modo offline. Há um custo para isso, é claro. No Brasil, os preços atuais são os seguintes:

articles.title: S-Neo soll Investieren vereinfachen – doch jede Sparkasse macht eigene Regeln
articles.text:
S-Neo: Sparkassen fordern Trade Republic und Scalable heraus – haben aber einen Nachteil
Die deutschen Sparkassen steigen in den hart umkämpften Brokerage-Markt ein.
Mit „S-Neo“ starten sie eine eigene Broker-App, die erfolgreichen Neobrokern wie Trade Republic oder Scalable Capital Paroli bieten und junge Anleger:innen an die Sparkassen binden soll.
Was kann „S-Neo“?
Mit „S-Neo“ können Kund:innen seit dieser Woche mit mehr als 21.000 Wertpapieren wie ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds) handeln – direkt in der Sparkassen-App. Depotführung und Wertpapierkauf werden dabei ebenfalls direkt in der App bereitgestellt.
Zunächst richtet sich das Angebot allein an Bestandskund:innen. Laut Angaben der Sparkassen hat rund die Hälfte der 20 Millionen App-Nutzer:innen noch kein Wertpapierdepot. Zum Jahreswechsel 2026/2027 wird S-Neo dann auch für Neukund:innen geöffnet.
Wie teuer S-Neo ist, entscheidet jede der bundesweit 338 Sparkassen selbst. Die Preise werden sich aber am marktüblichen Standard von Neobrokern wie Trade Republic, Scalable Capital oder Revolut orientieren, die den Wertpapierhandel per Smartphone salonfähig gemacht haben.
Bei den meisten Sparkassen werden Depotführung und Ausführung von Sparplänen in der Regel kostenlos sein. Allerdings ist die kostenlose Depotführung bei einigen Sparkassen begrenzt und gilt nur bis zu einem bestimmten Höchstbetrag. Die Transaktionsgebühr liegt meist zwischen 95 Cent und einem Euro.
Bei den Sparkassen funktionierte der Wertpapierhandel bislang nur über den S-Broker und war auch im Vergleich zu Online-Banken eher teuer. Dass für S-Neo eine zentrale Übersicht der Konditionen fehlt, schwächt die Vergleichbarkeit des Angebots und könnte neue Kund:innen abschrecken.
Der Präsident des Deutschen Sparkassen- und Giroverbandes (DSGV), Ulrich Reuter, hatte noch vor dem Start hohe Erwartungen an das eigene Brokerage-Angebot formuliert. Er glaube, „dass wir im Gesamtpaket besser sein werden als jeder heutige Neo-Broker“.
S-Neo: Start in einen umkämpften Markt
Mit dem neuen Angebot starten die Sparkassen allerdings spät in einen umkämpften Markt, den die Neobroker vor Jahren erschlossen haben. Anbieter wie Trade Republic, Scalable Capital oder Revolut haben den Wertpapierhandel über das Smartphone salonfähig gemacht und vor allem junge Anleger:innen an den Kapitalmarkt herangeführt. Auch bei ihnen sind Sparpläne und die Depotführung oft kostenlos und die Transaktionsgebühren liegen ebenfalls bei rund einem Euro.
Die Neobroker haben ihr Geschäftsmodell seitdem aber stark weiterentwickelt und bieten etwa neben Aktien-Sparplänen auch Zinsen auf das Verrechnungskonto oder den Handel mit Kryptowährungen an.
Zum Start setzen die Sparkassen auf eine breit angelegte Werbe-Kampagne mit der Webvideo-Serie „Die Neusparer“, die auf Joyn, RTL+, Amazon Prime sowie auf Instagram, Facebook, Tiktok und Youtube zu finden ist. Ob die Geschichten, die im mittelfränkischen Spardorf spielen, wirklich junge Anleger:innen für die App begeistern, wird sich zeigen.

articles.title: Marvel Tōkon is scratching my Marvel vs. Capcom itch so far
articles.text:
Some of my fondest gaming memories come from Marvel fighting games.
Spending far too many quarters on Marvel vs. Capcom 2 in arcades. Messing around with the oft-forgotten Marvel Nemesis on PSP with some friends. Having some of my first-ever online gaming experiences being in Marvel vs. Capcom 3 on PS3. I’ve never been much of a fighting game guy overall due to how complex they can be, but MvC always spoke to me, especially when the third game introduced a “Simple” mode to streamline inputs.
All of that is to say that the lack of a new Marvel vs. Capcom since 2017’s somewhat underwhelming Infinite has been a real bummer. Imagine how pleasantly surprised I was, then, when Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls was unveiled last year by PlayStation. Not only is it a brand-new Marvel fighter, but it’s being developed by Arc System Works, the fan-favourite Japanese studio behind the likes of Guilty Gear, BlazBlue and Dragon Ball FighterZ. And after spending an hour with Tōkon earlier this month at PlayStation Canada’s offices, I’ve come away very pleased with how it’s shaping up.
First and foremost, it should be stressed that Tōkon isn’t really like Marvel vs. Capcom. It’s similar insofar as it’s also a 2D fighting game that features Marvel characters who can tag in and out of matches, but naturally, it also has many of its own mechanics and combo systems that create its own distinct feel.
The biggest difference is the approach to tag-teaming. Where MvC was about swapping between teams of three (or two in Infinite) with their own health bars, Tōkon features parties of four that all share HP. This means that you go into a match selecting a party leader and three assist characters from a total launch roster of 20, although you can freely swap between them at any time.
It took some getting used to at first, but I came to appreciate this unique approach. For one, it creates these gloriously stylish comic book page-inspired vs. screens that segue into the respective party leaders having fun bits of trash talk, like the plucky teenager Ms. Marvel roasting Wolverine, a grown man, for being as short as she is. The game also assigns a random name to your team depending on who’s a part of it, although some of them are a bit weird, like “Genius Geniuses” for one that included Iron Man.
And on a deeper level, having four characters who share a health bar challenged me to rethink my approach to using them. It was less like an RPG-style party of characters and more like different weapons in my loadout; my health remains the same no matter which I use, but swapping between them still presents opportunities to change tactics on the fly. This was especially valuable as I was getting used to the characters, quickly realizing who I favoured over those I wasn’t as good with.
The demo also had 14 of the total 20 characters to try out, and I was impressed by the variety of their move sets. Spider-Man plays as fast as you’d hope, with a neat twist that his Spider-Sense gives him unique counters and flashy animations. Meanwhile, Danger (the physical robot manifestation of the X-Men’s Danger Room, funny enough) has a Mega Man-esque arm cannon that can shoot missiles and lasers for more ranged play. I was especially pleased to see the inclusion of Ms. Marvel, one of my favourite characters who is a blast to play thanks to her embiggened punches and kicks that afford her some excellent zoning potential.
But surprisingly, my favourite character was the lesser-known Magik, the Russian warrior who was played by Anya Taylor-Joy in the oft-forgotten X-Men spin-off, The New Mutants. Despite wielding a huge Buster Sword-like blade, she swings it with speed and agility that fondly reminded me of my MvC main Dante, with the added bonus of her being able to tap into even more demonic fire-based abilities.
All in all, the roster is quite diverse, and the fact that it even has several X-Men characters, like Wolverine, Magneto and Storm, is already a huge improvement from their inexcusable absence in MvC Infinite. Further, I loved how many of the characters are being voiced by returning Marvel stars like Josh Keaton (The Spectacular Spider-Man) as everyone’s favourite wall-crawler, Steve Blum (Wolverine and the X-Men) as Wolverine (plus Green Goblin, reprising the role from The Spectacular Spider-Man) and Nolan North (Deadpool) as the Merc with a Mouth. With all of that said, only 20 characters at launch feels a bit thin, especially when the past few MvC games had at least 30 to start.
The only big question mark that remains for me is the story. Generally, you shouldn’t expect much from a fighting game narrative, even though there’s a lot of inherent potential in a silly, fun crossover such as this. And so far, Tōkon‘s premise sounds fairly generic, with the relatively obscure comics character known as the Champion recruiting teams of heroes and villains to compete in a tournament for his own amusement. That said, the story was penned by Kieron Gillen, a prolific writer behind Marvel comics like Uncanny X-Men and Young Avengers, who also once worked in video game journalism and even co-founded Rock Paper Shotgun. That extensive background makes me hopeful he’ll bring something worthwhile to the narrative.
But for now, I’m loving what I’ve played of Marvel Tōkon. With its diverse roster and unique focus on 4v4 matches, I can’t wait to play more. And thankfully, we won’t have to wait long, either. An open beta runs from July 24 to 26 on PS5 and PC ahead of the game’s launch on August 6.

articles.title: ASML Considers Price Increase for Low-NA EUV, TSMC Unhappy
articles.text: According to the latest information from the second quarter financial results, ASML is considering raising prices for its Low-NA EUV tools, which is reportedly upsetting its customers. ASML CFO Roger Dassen has noted that the company is looking into price increases for these tools, aligning its pricing strategy with product value. As the company continues to enhance the productivity of its tools, ASML plans to adjust pricing accordingly. The company operates a business unit called Installed Base Management, which focuses on maintaining and improving existing machines. Most of the recent productivity gains have come from ASML's software that operates EUV machines, and the company recently confirmed that: ASML CFO Roger Dassen When it comes to Low-NA pricing, of course, you know that we keep on increasing the productivity of the Low-NA tool. Of course, that gives us a pretty strong runway for potential price improvements going forward... Value-based pricing is the concept that we follow within ASML. In the current environment, of course, the value for customers is higher than in other circumstances. Read full story

articles.title: The Download: Chinese AI divides the White House, and a record copyright payout
articles.text:
The Download: Chinese AI divides the White House, and a record copyright payout
Plus: Anthropic's record $1.5 billion copyright settlement has been approved.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself
Last weekend, several current and former advisers to President Donald Trump on AI publicly lobbed insults at the country’s leading AI companies. David Sacks branded Anthropic’s models “lobotomized” and “woke.” Emil Michael, a top Pentagon official, called OpenAI’s new head of strategic futures a “supreme village idiot.”
It began because no one can agree on what to do about Kimi, a free, open-source model that Chinese AI company Moonshot launched last week. It appears to rival the intelligence of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which are very much not free.
Every time a new smart, free model from China gets released, US companies see less reason to fork out money for models from Anthropic or OpenAI. That’s creating economic and political problems for the president—and dividing the top AI strategists in his orbit.
Read the full story on why no one can agree what to do about Kimi.
—James O'Donnell
This article is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

+ Yet many authors and creators still don’t view it as a win. (TechCrunch)
+ But AI copyright anxiety could limit creativity. (MIT Technology Review)

It wants to stop the West from acquiring its tech and startups. (FT $)
+ Beijing has held talks with tech firms about potential restrictions. (Reuters $)

Chris Fall had led CAISI, the federal AI Safety Institute, since April. (Axios)
+ No reason was given for his exit. (CNBC)
 
5 Google is working on a new chip to run Gemini models more efficiently 
The chip, called “Frozen V2,” may be deployed in 2028. (Information $)
+ Alphabet stock popped on the report. (CNBC)

A draft drone manual paves the way for weaponised quadcopters. (404 Media)

The €550 million fine is the largest-ever under the Digital Services Act. (BBC)
+ Alibaba has vowed to appeal the fine. (SCMP)
8 Election advice from AI chatbots is “inaccurate and unreliable”
That’s the conclusion from tests in Hungary earlier this year. (Guardian)
9 Red light therapy is showing promise for healing and healthy aging
Better skin and reduced vision loss are also on the cards. (Economist $)
10 Neill Blomkamp’s new horror clip is all AI-generated—and it sucks
The acclaimed director wants to make “a full feature in this format.” (Gizmodo)
Quote of the day
“This would be a terribly self-defeating form of intervention if it were to happen.”
—Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya slams plans to restrict Chinese AI models in a post on X.
One More Thing
Inside Chicago’s surveillance panopticon
  Early on the morning of September 2, 2024, four people were shot and killed on a westbound train in Chicago. Police swiftly activated a digital dragnet—a surveillance network that connects thousands of cameras across the city—and arrested the suspect just 90 minutes later.
Law enforcement and security advocates say this vast monitoring system protects public safety and works well. But activists and many residents say it's a surveillance panopticon that creates a chilling effect on behavior and violates guarantees of privacy and free speech.
Go inside the surveillance network that’s dividing Chicago.
—Rod McCullom

articles.title: The Light Flip is a minimalist flip phone with a point to prove
articles.text:
A few years ago, the team at Light shipped the most smartphone-like device they’d ever created. The Light Phone III still kept to its minimalist, no-distractions ethos, but it was a phone-size rectangle with a phone-size touchscreen, a camera, and a number of other features. Some people loved having an almost-smartphone, but Kaiwei Tang, Light’s cofounder, says he started getting feedback he didn’t expect. Lots of users, particularly young ones, didn’t want a smartphone. More than that, actually: They didn’t even want something that looked like a smartphone. “We have users who tell us, ‘Hey, I hate smartphones. I don’t want to be seen using a smartphone,’” Tang says. Then they’d almost always ask for the same thing: a Light Phone, but a flip phone.
The Light Flip is a minimalist flip phone with a point to prove
It’s not quite a dumbphone, but it’s definitely not a smartphone. And that’s kind of the whole point.
It’s not quite a dumbphone, but it’s definitely not a smartphone. And that’s kind of the whole point.
So Light made a flip phone, set to ship early next year. “The Light Phone in flip phone form” is even roughly the right way to think about it. This one comes in a bunch of colors – a big departure from the all-black Phone III — but keeps Light’s chunky vibes. There’s a 2.8-inch screen on the top half, but it’s not a touchscreen; all the interaction comes via the bottom half’s standard numberpad, D-pad, and function buttons. The whole thing is powered by a MediaTek MT8873 processor, 128GB of storage, and 6GB of RAM. There’s a USB-C port for charging, a headphone jack for headphones, a single camera on the back, a notification light on the front cover that glows when there’s something for you to see, and not much else.
Early in the process, Tang says, Light decided to really emphasize the flipping of the flip phone. The team opted not to put any kind of screen on the outside of the device, wanting to make sure you had to deliberately open up the device. Tang says he loved “this action of opening up your technology, and then you close it down and it goes away.”
He says the Light Flip is designed mostly as a second phone, not so much to replace your iPhone or Galaxy device entirely but to give you an easy way to leave it at home. That was the idea behind the Light Phone III, too, but that was a hard sell for a $699 device — Tang says most of the negative feedback he’s heard about the Phone III was about its cost. The Light Flip is comparatively priced to move: You can buy it for $299, or you can pay $39 a month for a Light Flip connected to Light’s cell service, and after 24 months, the phone is yours.
The software in the Light Flip is the same LightOS as the Light Phone III — Tang says the only thing this new device can’t do is tap-to-pay, since there’s no NFC chip inside. Everything else, from camera to notes to navigation, should work just the same. And as of recently, you can add to the device’s software yourself: Light recently released an SDK for its app “toolbox,” so you can write apps for your own device or submit them to a broader app library.
Letting other people write Light software is a long time coming. Some Light Phone III users resorted to hacking full-fledged Android on the device, just to run the apps they wanted. The whole thing seems to have taken Tang time to get used to. But he knows Light can’t build all the software people need, and he’s found a way to help users solve their problems without inflicting the solutions on everyone else. “You own the device,” Tang says. “You own your software at the same time. Obviously, I don’t want to see people using social media on our phone, but that’s my problem. That’s your phone, you should be able to do whatever you want.”
Tang says he expects developers will hack their AI agents into LightOS and will create ways to communicate with their OpenClaw-running Mac Minis at home. He’s not worrying about it, nor is he particularly interested in making it easier. “When I interview young people,” he says,
“one thing that never comes up? No one wants an AI button on their phone.” In fact, he says, it’s the opposite: More and more users want him to guarantee there’s no AI anywhere in the Light universe.
In a way, the Light Flip is a nod toward retro nostalgia, a long-gone era before our phones were huge screens that demanded all of our attention all the time. But Tang says he doesn’t see it that way — he thinks flip phones got thrown away far too soon. “This form factor, young people have never experienced it,” he says. “They love the idea of closing it, and it goes away.” As poll after poll shows people revolting against the incursion of AI into their lives, and more and more people find themselves looking for a way out of their relationship with their smartphones and their feeds, Light Phone has decided to take on the smartphone not by trying to sneakily replace it but by building something that no one would ever mistake for a smartphone. That might be its best feature.

articles.title: Gritt exits stealth with $32 million for robots to build solar plants — then, everything else | TechCrunch
articles.text:
One of the most important things happening on Earth today is the solar energy build-out. Around the world, companies and countries are racing to deploy solar and batteries to achieve energy independence and limit the effects of climate change.
That build-out, though, is running into a labor market challenge, with a limited supply of workers to meet a growing demand for installation. Robots could be an answer, but industrial robots have historically struggled in unstructured environments, at least until now. The latest generation of AI models may have changed that equation.
That’s the driving idea behind Gritt, a startup founded by two Carnegie Mellon-trained roboticists, CEO Puneet Puri and CTO Vishal Dugar. The company exited stealth Tuesday morning with a $26 million Series A round of funding led by Obvious Ventures, with participation from Union Square Ventures and Active Impact Investment. That brings its total funding to $32 million, following an earlier seed round backed by First Round Capital, Climactic, Congruent Ventures, and VSC Ventures. The startup is building an intelligent system to “help civilization build infrastructure faster,” in Puri’s words.
“Our thesis is that if we truly want to speed up construction,” Puri tells TechCrunch, “you need an intelligence which can work in the outdoor, chaotic environments of these construction sites, and it has to be generalizable enough that it can work in these varied environments.”
Rather than building its own robots from scratch, Gritt uses off-the-shelf hardware — thus far, rented skidders and robotic arms built by companies like Kawasaki — to build platforms that are controlled by its AI models. The first job its systems handle is unloading large, glass solar panels, carrying them toward the metal frames where they need to be installed, and positioning them on the frames with sub-millimeter accuracy so workers can fasten them.
“There are people who used to build rockets that went into space and had infinite budget for the smallest little part, and then there are people who know what it means to get into dirty, dull, and dangerous jobs and scale them like mad,” said Andrew Beebe, the partner at Obvious Ventures who led Gritt’s Series A round. “These guys are in the second camp, and that’s a special kind of entrepreneur that has the technical chops, the AI, and the machine vision skills to make it work.”
Gritt has two systems currently deployed in the field, using the data they collect to improve their behavior. Puri says that a typical eight-person crew can install 800 panels a day, but the same crew working with Gritt’s systems can install 3,000 to 4,000 panels each day.
Now, the company says it is contracted to help install 2.8 gigawatts of solar panels in the next 18 months, and that its customers include three of the top 10 U.S. power construction companies. The company hopes to be operating 48 of its systems within the next six months.
TechCrunch spoke to one Gritt customer who declined to be identified for competitive reasons, but who was enthusiastic about the system’s ability to improve his work. He expects it to be easier to work at remote sites where it is difficult to attract workers, and anticipates a reduction in injuries since workers won’t have to repeatedly lift 100-pound panels overhead.
Gritt is competing against companies with their own panel-installing robots like Luminous Robotics, Cosmic, and China’s Trinabot. Those companies are building their own hardware, rather than focusing on off-the-shelf vehicles and arms like Gritt, a difference that could shape who grows faster and with a leaner cost structure as demand grows.
Gritt wants to add new manipulation tasks to its system so it can fasten the solar panels, drill posts, and even build the racks they sit on. Longer term, it also wants to move into other common, labor-intensive construction tasks, like tying rebar before concrete is poured over it.
What’s enabled the startup to pursue this vision? Mainly, the rise of new AI models, the founders say.
“Making a system for one solution was still possible to some extent five years ago, right?” Puri said, but AI is now making that work generalizable — the same underlying pipeline can be reused and improve across tasks. As an example, he noted that training the system to stack cinder blocks took weeks, while a similar demo with rebar tying took just a day using the same software.
But training new tasks is just the beginning of Gritt’s vision. The founders believe the suite of sensors and intelligence its systems bring to worksites can do more than install panels; it can boost management and decision-making. For instance, they imagine their system noticing a trench is open while a storm approaches, allowing it to alert workers to cover it before rain damages components, or flagging missing inventory.
“Gritt becomes now this layer of physical AI, which is doing this dextrous, labor-intensive task, plus it can help you take decisions on the site,” Puri said.

articles.title: MIT to Become Hotbed of AI Video Surveillance - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
MIT to Become Hotbed of AI Video Surveillance

According to information obtained by The Tech, MIT is spending over $3 million on more than 500 AI surveillance cameras in academic buildings, residence halls, and outdoor areas along Memorial Drive. articles.title: AliExpress hit with record $625M fine after failing to make EU-ordered fixes
articles.text:
Yesterday, the European Commission slapped AliExpress with the largest fine yet under the Digital Services Act (DSA), exceeding $625 million.
In a press release, the EC said that AliExpress failed to “diligently assess and mitigate risks relating to the sale of illegal, unsafe, or counterfeit products on its e-commerce platform.”
Officials found that AliExpress not only failed to staff teams dedicated to removing counterfeit and dangerous items from the platform, but it also made it easy for bad actors to evade detection.
Staff was so limited that some content moderators were sometimes given just “tens of seconds” to evaluate if a flagged product met EU standards, The Guardian reported. The result, the EC said, was that it “found millions of products that reappeared online” after being flagged for removal, “which sometimes stayed for longer than a month.”
Bad actors can easily skirt AliExpress safeguards, the EC said. All some sellers had to do to circumvent automatic takedowns was miscategorize their products so that fewer checks were required before posting dangerous goods.
For shady sellers, the risks of detection appeared low. The e-commerce site’s mandatory brand authorization system was also ineffective and understaffed, the EC found, and AliExpress did not penalize traders for selling illegal products as its policy claims it would.
Making things worse, AliExpress “inadequately assessed how its recommender and advertising systems exacerbate the spread of illegal products,” the EC said. So rather than remove illegal products, AliExpress was recommending them to consumers and helping to maximize exposure. Talking to the press, the European Union’s tech chief, Henna Virkkunen, noted that one in five Europeans shop monthly at retail sites like AliExpress, Temu, and Shein.
AliExpress also relied on a single quantitative metric to gauge how effectively its systems were working to weed out illegal products. And that metric did not properly measure the extent of the harm. EC testing found that “a high volume of illegal products”—including unsafe toys and dangerous cosmetics—“continued to circulate despite AliExpress’ moderation efforts.”

articles.title: Dutch chip sector at very high risk of Chinese interference, government-funded study warns — calls for stricter vetting at sites like ASML
articles.text:
Dutch chip sector at very high risk of Chinese interference, government-funded study warns — calls for stricter vetting at sites like ASML
Semiconductors ranked above maritime and aerospace in the government-funded risk assessment.
The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies has rated the Dutch semiconductor industry as being at very high risk of Chinese foreign interference in a recent report, placing it above the maritime and aerospace sectors, and citing years of espionage against ASML and NXP. Written by Benedetta Girardi and Hans Horan for the China Knowledge Network, a body funded by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the study calls for stricter vetting of personnel at sensitive chip sites and a public-private fund to swap out high-risk foreign hardware, including server motherboards and baseboard management controllers. Both authors expanded on the findings in interviews with Nikkei Asia last week.
The report sorts Beijing's methods into five categories: economic statecraft, digital and information operations, physical interference, legal pressure, and talent-based technological espionage. ASML said in 2023 that a former China-based employee stole data about its lithography tools from an internal product lifecycle management system, one of several insider theft cases at the company stretching back to 2015, and the Dutch military intelligence service MIVD named all three sectors as Chinese espionage targets in its 2024 annual report.
China restricted rare earth exports through 2025, and ASML's complex optical systems depend on those materials. The EU holds an anti-coercion instrument designed to counter economic blackmail by non-member states, but leaders treat it as a last resort. The tool was "created with China in mind," Benedetta Girardi, program coordinator of the HCSS Europe in the Indo-Pacific program, told Nikkei Asia.
Dutch anti-discrimination law prohibits screening policies that target only Chinese nationals, and the standard VOG background certificate doesn't account for an applicant's conduct or connections outside the EU. The report proposes a tiered system instead, whereby companies identify their "he Hague Centre for Strategic Studies has rated the Dutch semiconductor industry as being at very high risk of Chinese foreign interferencejewels" and apply deeper screening, weighing factors such as susceptibility to blackmail or bribery, to staff with direct access, while junior hires and contractors get lighter checks.
A proposed resilience fund, built with the EU and NATO, would pay to replace equipment such as server motherboards, BMCs, and large ship-to-shore cranes with European-made equivalents. The mechanism would sit alongside Project Beethoven, the €2.5 billion Dutch government effort to expand domestic semiconductor production capacity, and would include surge funding that unlocks during crises such as sanctions escalation or major cyber campaigns.
ASML denied a U.S. government concern in June that one of its EUV machines had reached China in breach of export controls, telling Tom's Hardware the claims were baseless and harmful to its reputation.
The Nexperia dispute, in which the Dutch government seized the chipmaker from its Chinese parent, and Beijing responded by blocking exports from its Guangdong site, played out while the report was being written. In a crisis such as a confrontation over Taiwan, the researchers assess that Chinese leverage over strategic industries would likely constrain Dutch policy choices and limit participation in allied responses.

articles.title: Apple la lía con iOS 27. Acaba de revelar el secreto mejor guardado de su próximo iPhone estrella
articles.text:
Apple acaba de cometer un error de novato. La última beta de iOS 27 (el SO que se lanzará oficialmente en septiembre) tiene información en clave que revela uno de los acontecimientos históricos de la compañía. Ese mismo que las filtraciones llevan adelantando durante meses, pero ahora con un toque totalmente oficial que llega de la mismísima Apple. ¿Qué revela iOS 27? Que en septiembre habrá un nuevo modelo de iPhone con una característica clave.
Desde Macworld han descubierto que iOS 27 tiene un mensaje en su código un tanto revelador. Está relacionado con la batería, y cuenta una de las claves del iPhone más esperado del año. Hablamos, cómo no, del Ultra. El modelo plegable que Apple no había confirmado, pero que todos los filtradores de la industria han mencionado como el lanzamiento estrella del mes de septiembre.
¿Qué se le ha escapado a Apple? Pues bien, en la beta de iOS 27 se puede leer un mensaje clave sobre la batería del supuesto iPhone Ultra. En la sección de ajustes ahora se pueden leer dos frases clave: "las baterías de este iPhone" y "una de las baterías". Ambas, dentro de la sección del estado de la batería ya conocido por todos los usuarios.
La clave está en el uso del plural. iOS 27 revela que está preparado para incluirse en dispositivos con varias celdas, algo que hace referencia directa al iPhone Ultra plegable. Estos dispositivos suelen tener dos baterías separadas en cada parte y unidas por un flex que pasa por la bisagra.
Hasta el momento, todos los iPhone de la historia han tenido una sola batería en su interior, y no se espera que esto cambie en el iPhone 18 o los modelos Pro: Apple reutilizará el diseño del año pasado, el chasis y buena parte de los componentes, por lo que esta nueva doble batería solo puede significar que estamos ante un nuevo modelo.
¿Significa esto que cambiar la batería del iPhone Ultra será más caro? iOS 27 hace saltar la alarma
No hay duda: tener dos baterías separadas complica las cosas. Para empezar, el propio componente es más caro por el hecho de estar separado en dos partes. También debe haber más sensores de temperatura y la novedad de un cable que las une. Ahora bien, la diferencia no debería ser dramática para el bolsillo.
El verdadero problema de tener dos baterías está en el coste y la complejidad de la sustitución. Si hacemos caso a iOS 27, es bastante probable que para cambiar la batería del iPhone Ultra sea necesario desmontar más piezas y, por lo tanto, que el tiempo invertido sea mayor.
Respondiendo a la pregunta: sí, es bastante probable que cambiar la batería doble del iPhone Ultra sea más caro. Además, iOS 27 deja otra cosa clara: el sistema sabrá reconocer cuando una de las dos baterías no sea original, por lo que no podrás cambiar solo una parte y "engañar" al dispositivo.
Con este descuido de la compañía, todo apunta a que en septiembre tendremos un móvil plegable en el catálogo, y también que este contará con la clásica doble batería que ya incluyen la mayoría de modelos similares de otros fabricantes.

articles.title: The Automotive Revolution: From Zonal Architecture to 48V - EE Times
articles.text:
The automotive industry is in the midst of a massive transformation. Over the past decade, cars are increasingly being equipped with advanced features that provide customers with greater safety, comfort, ease of use, and enjoyment. That includes everything from heated seats to infotainment screens, safety cameras to high-end sound systems. Some of the most innovative vehicles are fully self-driving cars and robotaxis.
All of these state-of-the-art additions to the driving experience require power — a lot of it. This means that the traditional 12V system that’s dominated the auto industry for the last 70 years must change to 48V to provide the high level of power needed. But in order to achieve this major shift, the industry first has to adopt a simplified, streamlined zonal architecture.
The Shift from Domain to Zonal Is Critical
Traditional domain architectures that group electronic control units (ECUs) by functionality rather than location are not optimized to handle the power requirements and safety features of 48V systems due to complex, heavy wiring harnesses; large communication delays; and numerous ECUs that require a great deal of space.
Zonal architecture, on the other hand, groups ECUs based on physical location, which allows for a simpler, lighter wiring harness; more deterministic delays; and centralized computing with greater integration. Moving from domain to zonal architecture will not only lead to increased energy efficiency, safety, and reliability — it will also pave the way toward a 48V transition that the auto industry is beginning to demand.
Your Partner in the Automotive Transition
MPS has consistently been at the forefront of technological innovation. We’ve been working on providing solutions to the automotive industry’s biggest challenges for years, long before those challenges were even recognized by the industry’s major players.
During that time, we’ve amassed deep knowledge that is enabling our product development. For example, the MPQ5884-AEC1, an 80V e-fuse, is ideal for zonal architecture because it delivers high current density in a very small package, provides faster response, protects against harmful voltage and temperature, and offers diagnostics and monitoring. Our system-level thinking encompasses the entire vehicle structure, making our current products inherently safer, smarter, and more efficient. Our roadmap of future products focuses heavily on zonal architecture and 48V.
We also have the expertise to help you design the ideal zonal architecture to meet the specific needs of your application. We’ll establish a close relationship with you, guiding you throughout your development process and serving as your advisor whenever we’re needed. Our breadth of understanding of the industry, coupled with our deep relationships with Tier 1 suppliers and automakers, make us an ideal partner as you navigate the transition to zonal architecture. We’re perfectly positioned to help you prepare for the ultimate conversion to a 48V future.

articles.title: Kenyan travel-fintech startup Afrinity joins FasterCapital’s EquityPilot programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Kenyan travel-fintech startup Afrinity has joined FasterCapital’s EquityPilot programme to help it refine execution priorities, strengthen go-to-market messaging, and align initial product milestones for early deployment and user acquisition.
Founded by Joseph Peters, Afrinity is a Nairobi-based platform that combines curated travel experiences across Africa with embedded fintech tools for savings, budgeting, currency conversion, and transactions. The platform focuses on community engagement and youth-driven content to promote authentic local experiences and economic participation.
It has now been selected for the EquityPilot programme run by FasterCapital, a global venture builder and online incubator dedicated to co-funding and co-founding innovative startups, which will focus in the first 30–60 days on refining execution priorities, strengthening go-to-market messaging, and aligning initial product milestones for early deployment and user acquisition.
“Afrinity aims to make African travel more discoverable and financially manageable while creating opportunities for local talent. We look forward to working with FasterCapital to prioritise the features that matter most to travelers and creators,” said RB Mwaurajr, founder and chairperson of Afrinity.

articles.title: Cette veste en cuir signée par Jensen Huang vaut officiellement 240 RTX 5090
articles.text:
Estimée au départ entre 40 000 et 60 000 dollars, l'une des iconiques vestes en cuir de Jensen Huang a finalement été adjugée à 960 000 dollars lors d'une vente aux enchères chapeautée par Sotheby's… c'est-à-dire 16 fois l'estimation la plus élevée initialement projetée.
L'une des vestes en cuir Tom Ford de Jensen Huang, patron de NVIDIA, a été vendue aux enchères pour 960 000 dollars ce 17 juillet -- soit l'équivalent de 240 RTX 5090 à leur prix actuel, s'est amusé à calculer VideoCardz.
La Jensen mania… pour la bonne cause
Estimée entre 40 000 et 60 000 dollars au départ, cette dernière a donc trouvé preneur à 16 fois son estimation initiale, après avoir fait l'objet de 65 enchères consécutives provenant de 45 collectionneurs différents, lit-on.
Si cette veste a autant plu aux collectionneurs, c'est évidemment parce qu'elle a été authentifiée, en l'occurrence par la société américaine Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA). On sait ainsi qu'elle a été portée par Jensen Huang le 18 octobre 2023 à Taipei, lors de l'évènement Hon Hai Tech Day organisé ce jour-là par le géant Foxconn.
De manière complémentaire, indépendamment de PSA, les spécialistes britanniques de James Spence Authentication ont par ailleurs vérifié et authentifié la signature du dirigeant de NVIDIA, apposée au feutre doré sur la doublure de cette veste. Quant à la provenance, elle est sûre, puisque émanant directement de Jensen Huang, a précisé Sotheby’s.
Une veste portée en 2023 chez Foxconn
Pour contexte, ce modèle précis de veste en cuir de la marque Tom Ford vaut entre 9 000 et 10 000 lorsqu'il est vendu neuf. Le prix de vente final de cette veste signée par Jensen Huang a donc atteint 100 fois le prix du neuf.
On apprend enfin que les 960 000 dollars de la vente, organisée par Long Journey Ventures, seront reversés à l’Edge Institute (une organisation à but non lucratif), pour le financement de bourses, de subventions et de résidences destinées à des personnes travaillant dans les domaines de la technologie, des sciences, et de la culture, notamment.
L'identité de l'acheteur, en revanche, n'a pas été dévoilée.

articles.title: Paytm Q1 net profit rises 79% in FY27
articles.text:
Paytm Q1 net profit rises 79% in FY27
The fintech company, which recorded positive momentum across all business segments, is leveraging AI deeply to drive productivity.
Fintech company Paytm has registered a 79% rise in net profit for the first quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 28%, on the back of broad-based growth across all business segments.
However, the stock markets have not reacted positively to these numbers. Paytm's stock price was down 2.14% on the National Stock Exchange on Tuesday morning trading.
The company reported a net profit of Rs 220 crore for the first quarter of FY27 compared to Rs 123 crore a year ago. Revenue touched Rs 2,448 crore, compared to Rs 1918 crore in the similar period a year ago.
Paytm attributed the first-quarter performance to the expansion of the merchant payments business, which accelerated market share gains and led to an increase in GMV (gross merchandise value). The performance was also driven by continued growth in the offline business and tailwinds in the online business, the company said.
According to the company, the merchant loan distribution continues to compound, led by a growing base, while AI-led capabilities drove gains in merchant engagement, retention, risk insights for partners, and strong collection efficiency. It said product innovation and AI optimised consumer acquisition resulted in market share gains in the consumer payment segment for five consecutive quarters.
Consumer monetisation saw strong growth led by distribution of postpaid service, personal loans, and wealth products.
On the role of artificial intelligence, Paytm said it has developed function specific models and agents by fine-tuning open source models to achieve higher efficiency and productivity.
A large addressable TAM and AI-led operating leverage have positioned Paytm for long-term sustainable profit growth, said the company.
The payment services business, which is the highest contributor to Paytm’s revenue at 56%, saw a 32% increase at Rs 1,384 crore. Revenue from distribution of financial services was Rs 814 crore, while revenue from marketing services was Rs 239 crore.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: España ha ganado el Mundial. Buena suerte buscando el vídeo exacto de ese momentazo que quieres volver a ver
articles.text:
España vuelve a ser campeona del mundo. Y una de las cuestiones que me ha asaltado esta mañana ha sido lo complicado que resulta, paradójicamente, encontrar momentos concretos de este Mundial 2026 en contraposición a lo fácil que resulta localizar los del Mundial 2010.
Es una cuestión que no tiene que ver con el marcador sino con cómo ha evolucionado Internet. Dentro de 16 años... ¿será tan fácil encontrar los momentos de 2026 como es ahora encontrar los de 2010?
La panorámica. En 2010, YouTube era el lugar del vídeo online. Cualquier grabación de la final de Sudáfrica, hecha con cámaras de TV o móviles, acababa subida ahí, indexada en una plataforma pensada para localizar vídeos concretos, con título y fecha.
En 2026 ese ejercicio es más difícil, y esa dificultad va a ir a más. El vídeo ya no vive en un sitio, ahora también vive en TikTok, en Instagram, en cuentas privadas, en historias que desaparecen tras 24 horas, en grupos de WhatsApp que nunca llegan al buscador.
Por qué es importante. Damos por hecho que grabamos y compartimos más que nunca, así que asumimos que todo queda archivado en algún sitio. No es así. Un aficionado graba el gol desde la grada con el móvil, lo sube a TikTok, se hace viral, una tele lo recorta para su informativo citando la fuente... y ahí se acaba el rastro.
- Puede que ese vídeo nunca llegue a YouTube.
- Puede que la cuenta que lo subió sea privada.
- Puede que no sea fácil de localizar a posteriori mediante el buscador de TikTok.
- Y puede que nunca llegue a quedar constancia de esa toma en otro lugar.
Entre líneas. Todas las plataformas se han convertido en plataformas de vídeo, pero cada una tiene un propósito y una línea editorial distintas, y eso hace que encontrar algo concreto sea una tarea más compleja. O imposible.
Es un fenómeno similar al que ha pasado con la búsqueda en texto, aunque por motivos distintos: contenido y comunidades se han repartido en fragmentos que no se comunican entre sí. El auge de las newsletters, comunidades encerradas en Discord o Telegram, etc.
- Un buscador centralizado indexa texto pensado para poder ser encontrado.
- Una app de vídeo efímero indexa atención inmediata, pero no memoria a largo plazo.
Son objetivos de diseño opuestos.
Sí, pero. Para el usuario ocasional es mucho más complicado localizar momentos en esta atomización. Para el usuario enganchado a plataformas concretas no lo es tanto porque sabe navegarlas y sabe dónde buscar dentro de cada una.
Eso significa que el problema no es solo tecnológico, sino de habilidad y de tiempo invertido en aprender la lógica de cada aplicación.
Y ahora qué. Dentro de 16 años, alguien querrá ver momentos de este Mundial, como el himno tocado por tubas, o el gol de Ferran grabado desde un asiento muy concreto. Si ese vídeo nunca llega a una plataforma con vocación de archivo, esa persona encontrará un hueco vacío. La memoria colectiva de ese Mundial dependerá en buena medida de decisiones editoriales que ninguna de las plataformas implicadas tomó pensando en el archivo, sino en el minuto en el que ese vídeo retenía atención.

articles.title: Avengers Doomsday vs Dune 3, le 18 décembre sera un jour crucial pour le cinéma
articles.text:
À vos agendas : le vendredi 18 décembre 2026 s’annonce déjà comme une journée historique pour l’industrie du septième art. Alors que Marvel Studios vient de lancer les hostilités en révélant la toute première bande-annonce explosive d’Avengers: Doomsday hier, le 20 juillet, la tension monte d’un cran.
Ce jour-là, deux géants absolus du cinéma mondial vont s’affronter directement dans les salles obscures : le film événement des frères Russo côté Marvel et Dune : Troisième partie (adapté du Messie de Dune) réalisé par Denis Villeneuve. Un choc frontal d’une ampleur inédite qui dépasse de loin le simple phénomène pop-culturel.
Le choc de deux visions du cinéma entre Avengers: Doomsday et Dune 3
Ce face-à-face met en scène la fracture qui traverse l’industrie hollywoodienne depuis cinq ans. D’un côté, Marvel joue son va-tout complet. Après une phase d’essoufflement critique, le studio ressort la très grosse artillerie : les frères Russo aux commandes, un casting pachydermique et la carte maîtresse du retour de Robert Downey Jr. sous le masque du Docteur Fatalis. L’objectif est limpide pour Disney : braquer le box-office mondial et prouver brutalement que la formule du Multivers en a encore dans le ventre.
De l’autre côté, Warner Bros. enfonce le clou avec la conclusion du Messie de Dune. Denis Villeneuve arrive en position de force, porté par une aura d’auteur désormais intouchable et un prestige visuel que la concurrence peine à égaler. On n’est plus du tout sur de la recette calibrée à la chaîne, mais sur une fresque monumentale, sombre et exigeante qui entend s’imposer comme le sommet de la science-fiction moderne.
La guerre fratricide des écrans géants
Au-delà de la bataille pour le cœur des spectateurs, ce vendredi 18 décembre sera le théâtre d’une bataille logistique féroce dans les coulisses des exploitants de salles.
Les deux longs-métrages ont été conçus spécifiquement pour être vus sur les plus grands écrans de la planète :
- L’IMAX verrouillé par Villeneuve : Dune 3 ayant réservé la date du 18 décembre en premier, la franchise de Warner a sécurisé la priorité sur les écrans IMAX 70 mm à travers le monde.
- La riposte Infinity Vision de Disney : incapable de monopoliser l’IMAX comme à son habitude, Marvel a dégainé sa propre certification premium maison, Infinity Vision, garantissant une présence massive sur les autres écrans géants Laser 4K et Dolby Cinema.
Jamais les cinémas n’auront eu à gérer un tel casse-tête de programmation pour répartir leurs salles d’exception entre deux blockbusters aussi gourmands en espace.
Un test ultime pour la fréquentation en salles
En 2026, alors que la fréquentation des cinémas cherche toujours son équilibre face à la concurrence féroce des plateformes de streaming, ce week-end de décembre fera office de crash-test ultime pour l’industrie avec Dune 3 d’un côté et Avengers Doomsday de l’autre.
Est-ce que le public aura le budget et le temps de s’enfiler deux mastodontes de près de trois heures chacun au cours du même week-end ? Ou est-ce que l’un des deux finira par cannibaliser les recettes de l’autre ? Réponse dans les salles le 18 décembre 2026. Une chose est certaine, le cinéma n’a jamais eu autant à jouer en une seule journée.

articles.title: Google repousse la sortie de sa plus puissante IA : ce gros défaut qui bloque tout en interne
articles.text:
C’est un retard à l’allumage qui commence à coûter cher à la firme de Mountain View, au point de faire trébucher l’action d’Alphabet de 4 % en bourse. Annoncée en grande pompe en mai dernier lors de la conférence annuelle Google I/O, la déclinaison la plus puissante de son modèle d’intelligence artificielle, Gemini 3.5 Pro, devait logiquement débarquer dans la foulée, courant juin 2026. Son rôle était d’épauler la version allégée baptisée Gemini 3.5 Flash. Plusieurs mois plus tard, le vaisseau amiral de Google brille toujours par son absence, et les raisons de ce blocage viennent d’être mises en lumière par une enquête de Bloomberg.
Le code informatique, talon d’Achille de l’IA
Si Google refuse pour le moment d’avancer la moindre date de sortie officielle, se contentant d’affirmer par la voix de ses porte-parole interrogés par CNBC que le modèle est toujours en phase de test auprès de certains partenaires, la réalité interne semble beaucoup plus tendue. Les ingénieurs et chercheurs de l’entreprise américaine seraient particulièrement déçus des capacités de Gemini 3.5 Pro en matière de programmation et de génération de code. Malgré une mise à jour massive des données d’entraînement effectuée à la fin du mois de juin, les résultats obtenus en laboratoire restent obstinément en deçà des exigences fixées par la direction.
Cette lacune technique tombe au plus mauvais moment pour le géant de la recherche. Le code informatique est en effet devenu le nerf de la guerre et le principal argument de vente pour monétiser l’IA auprès des développeurs et des entreprises. Pendant que Google patine, la concurrence avance à un rythme effréné. OpenAI vient de lancer son redoutable modèle GPT-5.6 Sol, revendiquant une efficacité technique supérieure sur les tâches de codage, tandis qu’Anthropic séduit les professionnels avec son puissant Fable 5. Même Meta est entré dans la danse la semaine dernière avec Muse Spark 1.1, présenté par ses équipes comme l’outil open-source le plus robuste pour le travail de développement autonome.
Une lourdeur administrative qui pèse sur l’innovation
Au-delà des simples obstacles techniques, ce retard mettrait également en lumière des problèmes d’organisation chroniques chez Alphabet. Le développement de l’écosystème Gemini implique aujourd’hui une multitude d’équipes et de décideurs, chacun cherchant à intégrer l’IA dans sa propre division, qu’il s’agisse de YouTube, de Maps ou du moteur de recherche. Cette multiplication des validations hiérarchiques ralentit considérablement la cadence de sortie des mises à jour.
Certaines voix en interne estiment d’ailleurs que l’objectif principal de Gemini ne devrait pas être la compétition acharnée sur la programmation destinée aux experts, mais plutôt l’amélioration directe des fonctions grand public, comme les fameux aperçus IA (AI Overviews) intégrés aux résultats de recherche. En attendant que Google tranche sa stratégie et parvienne à hisser son modèle au niveau de ses rivaux, l’entreprise demande à ses utilisateurs de s’armer de patience avec la version 3.1 actuelle.

articles.title: Rank launches finance products to expand access to capital
articles.text:
Rank, the Nigerian fintech formerly known as Moni, has launched three community-powered financial products, betting that digitising Africa’s traditional savings groups can provide a new route to zero-interest capital for individuals and small businesses.
Starting in Nigeria, the company unveiled Money Circles, a digital version of rotating savings groups; Tribe, which enables existing communities to manage shared finances; and Rank Perks, a payroll product offering salary-backed credit and workplace savings circles.
The launch targets a persistent financing gap in Nigeria, where only 4% of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) have access to formal bank loans. Rank is betting that digitising community-based finance can widen access to capital for entrepreneurs and workers who remain underserved by traditional lenders.
The launch comes eight months after Rank acquired group savings platform AjoMoney and Zazzau Microfinance Bank, now known as Rank Microfinance Bank. The acquisitions gave the company a regulated banking licence and strengthened its push beyond credit into savings, payments, and wealth management products centred on collective finance. The company said it has paid out more than $100 million to users across various communities in the past year.
“For generations, Africans have relied on communal financial structures to build wealth and acquire assets,” said Femi Iromini, CEO and co-founder of Rank. “We are bringing these trusted traditions into the modern age by layering cutting-edge technology, solving structural trust issues and turning collective financial habits into a modern, institutional-grade engine for generational wealth.”
Money Circles, one of its flagship products, digitises rotating savings schemes such as ajo, esusu, and other rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAs). According to the company, users can join a savings circle, contribute monthly, and receive a lump-sum payout when it is their turn. Rank noted that it charges a fixed service fee based on when a user receives their payout and guarantees payouts even if another member defaults.
The second product, Tribe, is aimed at existing communities such as families, friends, colleagues, and cooperatives. Rank said the product enables groups to manage rotating contributions and shared financial goals in one place while tracking every contribution and payout in real time.
Rank Perks, the last of the product launches, extends financial access into payroll. It allows employers to offer their staff salary-backed credit and company-wide savings circles, with repayments and contributions deducted automatically from monthly salaries.
Rank added that it introduced new features alongside the product launches, including everyday bank accounts, digital payment handles, and flexible and fixed savings options.
The company enters a competitive consumer finance market with players such as PiggyVest, Cowrywise, and other digital savings and wealth management platforms. However, its new products are community-focused, while other players focus on helping individuals save or invest. With these new products, Rank is attempting to digitise the informal savings systems that predated the rise of fintechs in the ecosystem.
“By combining our cultural heritage with digital-first security, we are giving young Africans the collective leverage they need to outpace inflation and securely build long-term equity,” Iromini said.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Le FBI arrête un jeune homme accusé d'avoir volé des cryptomonnaies via de faux jeux Steam.
articles.text:
Quand vous achetez un jeu sur Steam, vous avez juste envie de passer un bon moment. Jamais vous n’imaginez qu’il va vous faire perdre de l’argent. C’est pourtant ce qu’ont vécu plusieurs personnes entre mai 2024 et février 2026.
Le procédé utilisé par les hackers est bien rôdé. Sur les réseaux sociaux comme X (Twitter), Discord, LinkedIn ou encore Telegram, ils font la promotion d’un jeu vidéo. Il suscite votre curiosité et vous l’installez.
Sauf qu’il est accompagné d’un malware invisible. Ce dernier fouille votre PC pour en extraire un maximum de données sensibles, notamment les identifiants et mots de passe de vos portefeuilles de cryptomonnaie. Ils sont alors utilisés par les pirates pour voler votre argent. Selon le FBI, l’opération aurait touché 8 000 PC et rapporté 220 000 dollars (environ 193 000 euros) au groupe de cybercriminels.
Un suspect arrêté dans une affaire de vol de cryptomonnaie via de faux jeux Steam
Les documents de l’agence fédérale américaine ne mentionnent pas la plateforme sur laquelle se trouvaient les jeux infectés, dont on sait qu’ils sont au moins 8. Mais leurs titres, ainsi que des captures d’écran d’internautes, laissent peu de place au doute.
BlockBlasters, Dashverse, Lunara ou encore PirateFi. Ces jeux ont été retirés de Steam depuis, après être restés parfois un mois en accès libre. BlockBlasters aurait permis le vol de 150 000 dollars à lui seul, avec un nombre de victimes estimé entre 261 et 478. Dont le streamer RastalandTV, qui a malgré lui diffusé en direct la perte de 32 000 dollars en cryptomonnaies.
    À lire aussi : 
    Steam supprime un jeu d’horreur de son store pour votre sécurité
L’internaute avait été contacté par l’un des hackers sous prétexte de tester son jeu moyennant finances. Cherchant à récupérer des fonds pour le traitement de son cancer, il a accepté. La somme volée représentait les dons de ses spectateurs.
Âgé de 21 ans et résidant en Floride, le suspect arrêté par le FBI s’appelle Zyaire Dontaevious Zamarion Wilkins, ou Sibel.eth sur le Dark Web. Les enquêteurs sont remontés jusqu’à lui en reliant des bitcoins volés avec l’achat de plus de 150 cartes cadeaux Bitrefill. Une plateforme sur laquelle vous pouvez payer en cryptomonnaie. Les cartes de Wilkins ont servi à régler des commandes Uber Eats.
Le média américain WPLG Local 10 précise que le FBI a également identifié le développeur principal des malwares utilisés. Il n’a pas encore été officiellement inculpé à ce jour. Quant à Wilkins, il risque jusqu’à 10 ans de prison.
Si vous avez installé l’un de ces jeux, considérez votre machine comme compromise. Lancez une analyse antivirus complète, changez tous vos mots de passe depuis un appareil sain et transférez vos cryptomonnaies vers de nouveaux portefeuilles.
Utilisez-vous Google News (Actualités en France) ? Vous pouvez suivre vos médias favoris. Suivez Frandroid sur Google News (et Numerama).
